question: Define theft under Section 303 of the BNS. Explain its essential ingredients with Illustrations.
modelAnswer: Under s.303(1) (formerly s.378 IPC), whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, commits theft. The ingredients are: (1) dishonest intention (causing wrongful gain or wrongful loss) at the time of taking; (2) movable property — under Expl. 1, a thing attached to the earth becomes capable of theft once severed, and under Expl. 2 the severing act itself may be the theft (Illustration (a): cutting down Z's tree to take it); (3) the property must be in the possession of another — possession, not ownership, is protected, so an owner who takes his pawned watch without paying commits theft (Illustration (k)), whereas a warehouse-keeper who sells goods already entrusted to him commits criminal breach of trust, not theft, because the goods were in his own possession (Illustration (e)); property lying on a highroad, possessed by no one, cannot be stolen, though it can be misappropriated (Illustration (g)); (4) absence of consent, which may be express or implied and given by the possessor or an authorised person (Expl. 5) — a friend who borrows a book believing he has implied consent does not steal (Illustration (m)); and (5) moving the property in order to take it — the offence is complete on the slightest movement; causing an animal to move moves everything it carries (Expl. 4; Illustrations (b), (c)). A person who takes property in good faith believing it to be his own lacks dishonesty and does not commit theft (Illustration (p)). Under s.303(2), theft is punishable with up to three years, or fine, or both; on a second or subsequent conviction, rigorous imprisonment of not less than one year up to five years, and fine. A first offender who steals property worth less than ₹5,000 is punished with community service once the property or its value is returned. Theft is cognizable and non-bailable (but non-cognizable and bailable in the under-₹5,000 proviso case), and compoundable by the owner of the property.

question: Distinguish between theft, extortion, robbery and dacoity.
modelAnswer: Theft (s.303) is dishonestly moving movable property out of another's possession without consent. Extortion (s.308) is intentionally putting a person in fear of injury and thereby dishonestly inducing him to deliver property or a valuable security. The key differences between them: in theft the property is taken without consent; in extortion the victim delivers it, with consent obtained by fear. Theft applies only to movable property; extortion can extend to valuable securities and signed or sealed papers convertible into them. Force or fear is not an element of theft but is the essence of extortion. Robbery (s.309) is an aggravated form of either: theft becomes robbery when, in committing it or carrying away the property, the offender for that end voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, hurt or restraint; extortion becomes robbery when the offender is present, puts the victim in fear of instant death, hurt or restraint, and induces delivery then and there. The element of immediacy separates robbery from extortion — a threat of future harm, or a threat made from a distance, is extortion (s.309 Illustration (d)). Dacoity (s.310) is robbery committed or attempted conjointly by five or more persons, counting those present and aiding. Punishments rise accordingly: theft three years; extortion seven years; robbery rigorous imprisonment up to ten years (fourteen on a highway at night); dacoity life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and, if any dacoit commits murder, death, life or at least ten years for all of them.

question: What is 'snatching' under Section 304? Why was it introduced?
modelAnswer: Section 304 is a new offence. Under s.304(1), theft is snatching if, in order to commit theft, the offender suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes, secures, grabs or takes away any movable property from any person or from his possession. Under s.304(2), snatching is punishable with imprisonment of either description up to three years and fine; it is cognizable, non-bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The ingredients are: (1) an act amounting to theft; (2) sudden, quick or forcible seizure, securing, grabbing or taking away; (3) from a person or his possession. The IPC had no separate offence for this. Chain-snatching and mobile-phone snatching, often by persons on motorcycles, were charged either as simple theft — which many considered inadequate given the danger and fear involved — or as robbery, which requires hurt, wrongful restraint or fear of instant harm and was often difficult to prove. Section 304 fills that gap by recognising the sudden or forcible character of the taking, with a compulsory fine and non-bailability. If the snatcher also causes hurt (for example, by dragging the victim), the offence becomes robbery under s.309.

question: Distinguish between criminal misappropriation (Section 314) and criminal breach of trust (Section 316).
modelAnswer: Both involve dishonest appropriation of property that the accused did not take unlawfully in the first place, but they differ. (1) How the property came to the accused: in criminal misappropriation, it comes into his possession innocently or casually — by finding it, by mistake, or in good faith; in criminal breach of trust, it is entrusted to him, or he is given dominion over it. (2) Relationship: CBT involves a fiduciary relationship (trust) between the owner and the accused; misappropriation involves none. (3) Property: s.314 is limited to movable property; s.316 extends to any property. (4) Conduct: s.314 punishes dishonestly misappropriating or converting to one's own use; s.316 also covers dishonestly using or disposing of the property in violation of a legal direction or a contract governing the trust, or wilfully suffering another to do so. (5) Punishment: s.314 — not less than six months, up to two years, and fine; s.316 — five years for ordinary CBT, seven years for carriers, wharfingers, warehouse-keepers, clerks and servants, and life or ten years for public servants, bankers, merchants, factors, brokers, attorneys and agents. (6) Classification: s.314 is non-cognizable and bailable; s.316 is cognizable and non-bailable. Examples: a person who finds a wallet with the owner's address and keeps the cash commits misappropriation (s.314); a society treasurer who spends the society's funds on himself commits CBT (s.316).

question: Define cheating under Section 318. How is cheating distinguished from a mere breach of contract?
modelAnswer: Under s.318(1) (formerly s.415 IPC), a person cheats who, by deceiving any person, (i) fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property; or (ii) intentionally induces him to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property. The Explanation provides that a dishonest concealment of facts is a deception. The ingredients are: deception; inducement caused by that deception; and either delivery or retention of property with fraudulent or dishonest intent, or an act or omission causing or likely to cause harm. The distinction from breach of contract turns on the intention at the time of the inducement. If the accused had a dishonest or fraudulent intention from the very beginning — for example, taking an advance for goods he never meant to supply — it is cheating. If he genuinely intended to perform when he made the promise, but later failed or changed his mind, it is only a civil breach of contract. Illustration (g) makes this explicit: a person who takes money promising to deliver indigo, not intending to deliver, cheats; but if he intended to deliver at the time and later breaks the contract, he is liable only in a civil action. Punishments: s.318(2) up to three years (raised from one year under s.417 IPC); s.318(3) up to five years where the offender was bound to protect the victim's interest; s.318(4), the former s.420 IPC, up to seven years and fine where the cheating induces delivery of property or the making, alteration or destruction of a valuable security.

question: Explain 'stolen property' under Section 317 and the offences connected with it.
modelAnswer: Under s.317(1), stolen property is property whose possession has been transferred by theft, extortion, robbery or cheating, and property that has been criminally misappropriated or subject to criminal breach of trust — whether the transfer, misappropriation or breach took place in or outside India. Once such property comes back into the possession of a person legally entitled to it, it ceases to be stolen property. The BNS newly includes property obtained by cheating. The connected offences are: (2) dishonestly receiving or retaining stolen property knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen — up to three years, or fine, or both; (3) dishonestly receiving or retaining property known or believed to have been transferred by dacoity, or receiving stolen property from a person known or believed to belong to a gang of dacoits — life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and fine; (4) habitually receiving or dealing in stolen property — life or up to ten years, and fine; and (5) voluntarily assisting in concealing, disposing of or making away with stolen property — up to three years, or fine, or both. All are cognizable and non-bailable; (2) and (5) are compoundable by the owner of the property, while (3) and (4) are triable by a Court of Session. The mental element is important: the accused must know or have reason to believe the property is stolen — circumstances such as a grossly low price, absence of documents, or an unusual time and place of sale may give reason to believe.

question: Define mischief under Section 324 and explain the graded punishments introduced by the BNS.
modelAnswer: Under s.324(1) (formerly s.425 IPC), whoever, with intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property, or any change in property or its situation that destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or affects it injuriously, commits mischief. Under Explanation 1, the offender need not intend loss to the owner — intention or knowledge of wrongful loss to any person is enough. Under Explanation 2, mischief can be committed on property belonging to the offender himself, or jointly to him and others — as where a person scuttles his own insured ship to defraud the insurers (Illustration (e)) or shoots a jointly owned horse (Illustration (g)). The BNS grades the punishment: (2) basic mischief — up to six months, or fine, or both (raised from three months); (3) mischief causing loss or damage to any property, including Government or local authority property — up to one year; (4) loss or damage of ₹20,000 or more but less than ₹1 lakh — up to two years; (5) loss or damage of ₹1 lakh or more — up to five years; and (6) mischief after preparation for causing death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of these — up to five years and fine. Sub-sections (2)-(4) are non-cognizable, (5) and (6) cognizable; all are bailable. Sub-sections (2) and (4) are compoundable by the person suffering the loss where the only loss is to a private person. Aggravated forms relating to animals, water supply, public roads, drainage, navigation marks, landmarks, fire and explosives, and rail, aircraft and vessels are in ss.325-328.

question: Explain criminal trespass, house-trespass, lurking house-trespass and house-breaking.
modelAnswer: Criminal trespass (s.329(1)): entering into or upon property in another's possession with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy the person in possession; or, having entered lawfully, unlawfully remaining there with such intent. The intent is essential — an entry for another purpose, such as to assert a bona fide claim of right, is not criminal trespass. Punishment: up to three months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both (s.329(3)). House-trespass (s.329(2)): criminal trespass by entering or remaining in a building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling, or a building used as a place of worship or for custody of property; introducing any part of the body is enough (Explanation). Punishment: up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both (s.329(4)). Lurking house-trespass (s.330(1)): house-trespass after taking precautions to conceal it from a person who has a right to exclude or eject the trespasser. House-breaking (s.330(2)): house-trespass where the offender enters or quits in one of six ways — through a passage he or an abettor made; through a passage not intended for human entrance, or by scaling a wall; through a passage opened by means not intended by the occupier; by opening a lock; by using criminal force, assault or threat of assault; or through a passage he knew was fastened and which he or an abettor unfastened. The Illustrations cover entry through a hole in the wall, a port-hole, a window, a forced door, a latch lifted with wire, a found key, and forcing past a door-keeper. Punishment for lurking house-trespass and house-breaking is in s.331, graded from two years (basic) to fourteen years (by night to commit theft, or by night after preparation for hurt), and up to life where grievous hurt is caused or death or grievous hurt attempted. Sections 329(3) and (4) are compoundable by the person in possession.

question: Problem: A gives his car to B, a mechanic, for repair. B, without A's permission, sells the car's new stereo system and replaces it with an old one. Separately, C, A's driver, takes the car at night for a joyride without A's permission and returns it in the morning. Discuss the liability of B and C.
modelAnswer: B: A entrusted the car to B for repair, giving him dominion over it. By dishonestly selling the stereo and replacing it with an old one, B misappropriated part of the entrusted property and converted it to his own use, in violation of the implied contract under which he held the car. This is criminal breach of trust under s.316(1). B is not guilty of theft, because the car was in his own lawful possession, not taken out of A's possession (compare Illustration (e) to s.303). As a mechanic dealing with the property in the way of his business he may be treated as an agent, attracting s.316(5) (life or ten years); otherwise ordinary CBT under s.316(2) applies — up to five years, or fine, or both, compoundable by A with the court's permission. C: C is A's servant. Whether C commits theft depends on dishonest intention. Taking the car temporarily causes wrongful loss to A (the use of his car, fuel, wear and risk) and wrongful gain to C, and under s.2(38) a person loses wrongfully when he is wrongfully kept out of his property, not only when he is permanently deprived of it; the absence of consent is clear. If the car was in A's possession (for example, parked at A's house with the keys kept by A), C's taking it without consent with that dishonest intention is theft by a servant under s.306 — up to seven years and fine. If instead C had been entrusted with the car and its keys for his duties, the dishonest unauthorised use may be criminal breach of trust by a servant under s.316(4). Courts have been divided on whether a joyride with intent to return is 'dishonest'; the answer depends on the facts, especially the degree of wrongful loss caused.

question: Problem: Six men enter a farmhouse at 1 a.m. by breaking the back-door lock. Two stay outside as lookouts. Inside, they tie up the owner and take cash and jewellery. When the owner's son resists, one of them stabs and kills him. Discuss their liability.
modelAnswer: House-breaking: the men committed house-trespass by entering a dwelling with intent to commit an offence, and entered by opening a lock, which is house-breaking under s.330(2)(d); since it was after sunset and before sunrise, s.331 applies in its night-time forms. Robbery and dacoity: they committed theft of cash and jewellery, and in doing so voluntarily caused wrongful restraint by tying up the owner, so the theft is robbery under s.309(2). Since six persons conjointly committed the robbery — the two lookouts counting as persons present and aiding — every one of the six commits dacoity under s.310(1), punishable with life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and fine (s.310(2)). Murder in dacoity: one of them murdered the son in so committing dacoity. Under s.310(3), every one of the six — including the lookouts — is punishable with death, life imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment not less than ten years, and fine. The actual killer is also liable for murder under s.103. Minimum sentence: the offender who stabbed the son used a deadly weapon and caused death at the time of committing dacoity, so s.311 fixes a minimum of seven years for him (already exceeded by s.310(3)). Night house-breaking with violence: s.331(8) also applies, making every person jointly concerned in night house-breaking liable to life or ten years where any of them causes death or grievous hurt. All these offences are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session.

question: Explain the new features of Section 303 relating to repeat offenders and minor thefts.
modelAnswer: Section 303(2) keeps the basic punishment for theft from s.379 IPC — imprisonment of either description up to three years, or fine, or both — but adds two new rules. First, for repeat offenders: in the case of a second or subsequent conviction under s.303, the offender must be punished with rigorous imprisonment of not less than one year, which may extend to five years, and fine. This introduces a mandatory minimum and a higher maximum for habitual thieves. Second, for minor first-time thefts: under the proviso, where the value of the stolen property is less than ₹5,000 and the person is convicted for the first time, he shall, upon return of the value of the property or restoration of the stolen property, be punished with community service. Community service is a new form of punishment listed in s.4(f). This reflects a reformative approach: petty first-time offenders can make restitution and serve the community instead of going to prison. The First Schedule of the BNSS treats this proviso case as non-cognizable and bailable, while ordinary theft is cognizable and non-bailable. Theft remains compoundable by the owner of the property under BNSS s.359(1).

question: When is an employer liable for criminal breach of trust in respect of employees' provident fund and ESI contributions?
modelAnswer: Explanations 1 and 2 to s.316(1) create deemed entrustment. Under Explanation 1, an employer of an establishment — whether or not it is exempted under s.17 of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 — who deducts the employee's contribution from wages for credit to a Provident Fund or Family Pension Fund established by law, is deemed to have been entrusted with the amount deducted; if he defaults in paying it into the Fund in violation of that law, he is deemed to have dishonestly used the amount in violation of a direction of law. Explanation 2 applies the same rule to employees' contributions deducted for the Employees' State Insurance Fund under the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948. The effect is that the prosecution need not prove a separate act of entrustment or a dishonest intention: deduction plus non-payment in violation of the law amounts to criminal breach of trust. The employer is punishable under s.316(2) with up to five years, or fine, or both (cognizable and non-bailable), or more severely if he falls within s.316(4) or (5). The provision protects workers whose money is withheld from their wages but never reaches the fund meant for their social security.
